extracted.intended_audience: linguistics scholars, discourse analysts, and advanced students interested in media/news language
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for analyzing the language of news media, summarizing major theoretical frameworks (van Dijk, Fairclough, Bell, Conversation Analysis) and substantive criteria for studying news texts, interviews, and media discourse trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: CDA is a shared perspective (not a single school or methodology) with an explicit sociopolitical agenda and a concern to reveal the role of discourse in reproducing or challenging sociopolitical dominance; it has become the standard approach to media texts within European linguistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CDA to foreground questions of ideology and power in media texts; expect analysis to integrate social critique rather than merely formal description. Note that CDA can be adapted in varying degrees (many studies use only a subset of its social/linguistic apparatus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Dijk's integrated framework for news discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: A framework that integrates production and interpretation of discourse with textual analysis, proposed as an interdisciplinary theory of news in the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze news using thematic structure (topics and their organization), 'news schemata' (a syntax of news stories), and consider tree-diagramming discourse structure. Compare across languages and paper types; van Dijk's work includes large-scale corpora and case studies (e.g., racism in the press).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic structure and news schemata
rubrics_metrics.description: The thematic structure of a news story consists of its topics and their organization (broad semantic structure); 'news schemata' are the syntactic/formal categories into which news can be analyzed and their relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map topics and schemata (e.g., via tree diagrams) to reveal discourse organization. Analyze how these components (themes, subthemes) form the overall semantic and syntactic architecture of stories; use to compare story-types, genres, and cross-paper differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairclough's three-dimensional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Three levels for discourse analysis: (1) text analysis (vocabulary, syntax, cohesion, macrolevel structure), (2) analysis of discourse practice (production, interpretation, distribution; orders of discourse), and (3) analysis of social practice (discourse's role in society, institutions, culture, and relation to power/ideology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct multi-level analysis: close textual study combined with examination of production/distribution contexts and broader socio-political relations. Use Hallidayan functional tools for text analysis and social theory to interpret ideological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bell's production–story–audience triad
rubrics_metrics.description: Three central themes for analysing news: the multiple processes that produce media language, the notion of the news story (structure, order, viewpoint, values), and the role of the media audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the chain of production (sources, journalists, multiple editing stages), treat items as 'stories' with narrative shape rather than simple articles, and incorporate audience assumptions/roles in interpretation. Bell emphasizes journalist practice and editorial influence on text.

rubrics_metrics.name: News story structural components (summary, attribution, events, actors, setting, followup, commentary, background)
rubrics_metrics.description: News discourse can be analyzed in terms of summary (headline and lead), attribution, events, actors, setting (time, place), followup, commentary, and background; the lead sentence embodies the character of the story and news values drive structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and annotate these components in stories; note that leads summarize and often eschew chronological order. Use this schema to compare how different outlets prioritize components and to reveal embedded values and viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple hands and editorial stages in news production
rubrics_metrics.description: News discourse is typically the product of multiple hands: journalists use a range of spoken and written sources; stories then pass through multiple editing stages before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing features or intentions to 'the journalist', account for source material, editorial intervention, and institutional constraints. Analysis should consider production chains and institutional practices that shape textual outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation Analysis for broadcast interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Conversation Analysis to broadcast interviews to examine sequential organization, openings, participant roles, and the sociopolitical salience of content and participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze turn-taking, question–answer sequences, interview openings, and how journalists manage access/control. Use CA methods to reveal how interactional structures shape reported meaning and viewpoints (Clayman & Heritage; Greatbatch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on macro-level discourse structures over lower-level linguistics for media analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Research emphasizes macro-level discourse structures (themes, schemata, narrative organization) rather than phonological or narrow syntactic structures when the concern is ideology and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize analyses that reveal discourse organization, framing, and intertextuality for political/ideological effects; use lower-level linguistic features selectively to support claims about macro-discourse strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative variation across outlets and contexts (quality vs popular, First vs Third World)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in news discourse are often greater between 'quality' and 'popular' newspapers than between national contexts; some variation exists across First/Third World contexts but cross-linguistic similarities are prominent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include comparisons across newspaper types and audience orientations; be cautious attributing differences solely to national/cultural factors without controlling for genre and editorial style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trends in media discourse: marketization and conversationalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary trends include marketization (increasing use of promotional/advertising language across domains) and democratization/conversationalization (shifts toward increased informality in media discourse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for promotional lexis, formulae borrowed from advertising, and markers of informality/conversational style; analyze how these shifts affect representation, authority, and audience engagement (e.g., political discourse such as New Labour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality and hybridity of media genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Media genres are frequently intertextual or hybrid: discourse styles mix in the media (e.g., news mingling with opinion, advertising, or conversational elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify genre-mixing signals and trace source genres contributing to a text; analyze how hybridization affects interpretation, stance, and perceived objectivity or subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical coverage priorities and gaps (production and reception)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a relative dearth of research on the production of news language (how texts are produced in practice) and, to a lesser extent, on reception (how audiences interpret news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing studies, prioritize under-researched areas like newsroom practices, editorial decision-making, and audience reception studies; triangulate text analysis with interviews/ethnography and audience research where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corpus and comparative case-study methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-sample corpora and comparative case studies (e.g., van Dijk's international samples, studies of racism in the press) are productive for uncovering systematic discourse patterns and ideological biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ corpus methods for broad patterning and case studies for in-depth contextualized analysis; combine quantitative frequency analysis with qualitative close reading to substantiate claims about discourse practices.
